title: Google's Pause Point Anti-Doomscrolling Tool Expands Beyond Pixel 11
excerpt: The Digital Wellbeing feature, which imposes a 10-second pause before distracting apps open, has reached older Pixels and been spotted on a OnePlus 13R, ending its Pixel 11 exclusivity.
body:
• Pause Point, Google's Digital Wellbeing feature that forces a 10-second pause before a distracting app opens, is appearing beyond the Pixel 11 series.
  • Android Authority found the feature running on a OnePlus 13R on the ColorOS 17 beta, and it has already reached older Pixels through the Android 17 QPR1 update.
  • During the pause, users can do a breathing exercise, view favourite photos, set a timer or switch to another app; turning Pause Point off requires restarting the phone.
  • For readers: check Settings, then Digital Wellbeing, after your Android 17 update arrives - Google has given no fixed date for the wider rollout.

Google's anti-doomscrolling tool Pause Point is shedding its Pixel exclusivity. The Digital Wellbeing feature, which launched as a Pixel 11 exclusive with Android 17, is now reaching older Pixel phones and has been spotted running on a third-party device, according to reports citing Android Headlines and Android Authority.

Android Authority confirmed Pause Point running on a OnePlus 13R powered by the ColorOS 17 beta, Android Headlines reported. A feature appearing on a device with a customised Android skin suggests Google is preparing a general rollout for Android 17 handsets equipped with Digital Wellbeing, rather than holding it as a Pixel selling point.

How Pause Point works

Pause Point intervenes at the moment an app launches, not after time has been spent in it. When a user opens an app they have labelled distracting, the feature imposes a 10-second breather, according to WebProNews. During the pause, the user can do a short breathing exercise, view favourite photos, set a timer or switch to an alternative such as an audiobook app.

The friction is deliberate, and it extends to switching the feature off: disabling Pause Point requires restarting the phone, which prevents a quick override in a moment of weakness. Google announced the feature on May 12, 2026, describing it as a middle path between strict app timers and total lockouts. Existing Digital Wellbeing tools - app timers and usage dashboards - have been part of Android for years; Pause Point differs by acting before the scroll begins.

From Pixel exclusive to wider Android

The exclusivity was always conspicuous. Pause Point was positioned as part of the broader Android 17 release, yet an official support page confirmed availability only on the Pixel 11 series running Android 17 and later, and Google's support pages still list the Pixel 11 as the feature's primary home. Android 17 itself began rolling out in June 2026 to Pixel phones.

The loosening came in stages: first to older Pixel models through the Android 17 QPR1 update, and now, with the OnePlus sighting, beyond Google's own hardware. Exact device support remains tied to Android 17 updates and subsequent quarterly releases, and Google has not shared a precise schedule for the wider rollout. Users on compatible devices should see the option appear in Digital Wellbeing settings as the update propagates.

Why it matters

Pause Point is built on a simple behavioural premise: most doomscrolling starts on autopilot, and a short, unavoidable pause at launch gives the user a chance to choose differently. Whether a 10-second delay survives contact with real habits is an open question - app timers, which intervene later, are routinely overridden. Making the tool available on the phones people already own, rather than only on the newest Pixel, is what turns it from a launch feature into a genuine test of that premise at Android scale.

For anyone who wants the effect before their update arrives, Focus mode and app timers remain available in Digital Wellbeing today. Pause Point, when it lands, adds the one thing those tools lack: a pause before, not after.
